title: Key safety tests missed capability gains in new model Anthropic says it won't release - TCR 08/16/26
description:
Anthropic disclosed an unreleased "Model 2" more capable than anything it sells and raised its own misalignment rating from "very low" to "low," Z.ai's GLM-5.3 six-folded a coding benchmark from 4.6 to 28.3 on the reused 743B base through post-training alone, and MIT's Boyden lab imaged the electrical firing of a whole living zebrafish brain 200 times a second.

https://sharedsapience.com/the-century-report-august-16-2026/

0:00 Open and framing
0:42 Anthropic discloses an unreleased Model 2
4:36 GLM-5.3 jumps six-fold from post-training alone
8:10 Communities win the data-center siting fights
11:45 A microscope reads a whole living brain
14:33 Close

This episode covers Anthropic's saturated safety evaluations and its outside-scored Conceptual Reasoning Index, the GLM-5.3 open-weight post-training jump, the data-center siting fights across Marshall, Larbert, and Warsaw, the natural-gas price forecast bending the buildout toward solar and storage, MIT's whole-brain voltage microscope, and Waymo's 18-county California expansion.

Anthropic's August risk report does two unusual things at once: it discloses an internal model it says it will not release, and it moves the company's self-assigned misalignment rating up a notch, citing increased uncertainty. Underneath sit two admissions that compound - Claude now authors most of the code merged into Anthropic's production repositories, and the task-based evaluations the whole safety case rests on "no longer capture increases in models' capabilities." Read next to that, Z.ai's GLM-5.3 reached adjacent capability through a potentially cheaper door, producing a roughly six-fold jump on Terminal-Bench 3.0 from a reused base with post-training alone, then saying it would stage its weights behind a two-week safety review. On the ground, communities in Michigan, Scotland, and Poland won the ballots and planning fights deciding what gets built next to their hospitals and water tables, while a fresh forecast warned data-center gas demand could triple prices and bend the next round toward solar, storage, and geothermal. In Ed Boyden's MIT lab, a microscope read a whole living brain's electrical activity at millisecond resolution. The thread connecting them: the labs themselves now admit the measurement has to move outside the company that built it.
